stemBlocks.value: The area of a quadrilateral is 4x² − 20x + 25 cm². (a) Factorise the expression completely. (b) Hence determine the length of each side. (c) State the type of quadrilateral. (d) Calculate its perimeter.
Think first: Check first whether the expression is a perfect square — 4x² and 25 are both squares.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p094-q22 from workbook page 94.

solutionSteps.instruction: Test for a perfect square by taking the square roots of the first and last terms.

contentBlocks.value: √(4x²) = 2x and √25 = 5; the middle term should be 2 × 2x × 5 = 20x, and it is (with a minus sign)
Result: It is a perfect square

solutionSteps.instruction: Read off the side length, since both factors are equal.
Name the quadrilateral with four equal sides formed by two equal factors.
Multiply one side by 4 for the perimeter.

strategyBlocks.value: Recognise the perfect square, take the repeated factor as the side, identify the shape as a square and multiply the side by 4.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) (2x − 5)²  (b) each side = (2x − 5) cm  (c) a square  (d) perimeter = (8x − 20) cm

whyThisWorks.value: A trinomial of the form a² − 2ab + b² is exactly the expansion of (a − b)², so spotting the pattern factorises it in one step. Because both factors of the area are identical, the two sides of the quadrilateral are equal, which forces the shape to be a square and makes the perimeter four times one side.

commonErrors.misconception: Writing (2x − 5)(2x + 5), which expands to 4x² − 25 and has no middle term.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Writing (2x − 5)(2x + 5), which expands to 4x² − 25 and has no middle term.

commonErrors.misconception: Calling the shape a rectangle when the equal factors show it is a square.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Calling the shape a rectangle when the equal factors show it is a square.

commonErrors.misconception: Expanding 4(2x − 5) as 8x − 5 and losing the factor on the second term.

examTip.value: Before splitting the middle term, glance at the first and last terms: if both are perfect squares and the middle term is twice the product of their roots, the answer is a squared bracket and you save a whole method.
